opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, because on the surface it seems almost magical. You show the network a board in the middle of a game, with stones scattered everywhere, territory not settled yet, and it just spits out a number like "black wins with 62% probability." How could it possibly know that?

The way I think about it is that the value function is learning by bootstrapping backward from the end of the game. At the very end, judging who won is trivial: you count territory and you're done. A position one move before the end is almost as easy. So in principle, through self-play, you get this enormous dataset of positions paired with eventual outcomes, and the network is regressing toward "given positions that look like this, how often did the side to move end up winning?"

What's remarkable is what it has to internalize to do that well. It can't just count stones, because in the middlegame a group that looks big might actually be dead, or a group that looks weak might have enough eye space to live. So implicitly the network has to learn concepts like life and death, influence, the strength of groups, which areas are likely to become territory. Nobody hand-codes those. They emerge because they're predictive of the outcome.

The convolutional structure helps a lot here, too. Go has this nice translation-invariant local structure, where a shape in one corner means roughly the same thing as in another corner, and convolutions exploit that. Then as you stack layers you get larger receptive fields, so the network can reason about how a local fight connects to the whole-board situation.

And there's a subtle point I find really beautiful. The labels are incredibly noisy. A single game outcome is one bit of information, and it's attributed to every position in that game, including ones where the result was decided much later by a blunder. But when you average over millions of games, that noise washes out and you get a genuinely good estimate. It's a nice example of how a simple objective plus a lot of data can produce something that looks like intuition.

That's also why it pairs so well with search. The value function gives you a fast, fuzzy, intuitive judgment, the kind of "this feels good for black" that a strong human player has, and then Monte Carlo tree search refines it by actually reading out variations. Each one covers for the other's weaknesses. I think that combination of learned intuition plus explicit search is a template that matters well beyond Go.

r001.rationale: It says endgame positions are easy to judge and positions one move before the end are almost as easy, but does not explain that this is because the remaining search horizon is shorter.

r002.rationale: It describes learning backward from game outcomes through self-play, but does not say search propagates reliable late-game value estimates to intermediate positions.

r003.rationale: It describes the unsettled board and life-and-death challenges in the middlegame, but does not identify it as the hardest phase for judging who is winning.

fable-5.1.text:
So the first thing to understand is that the value function in something like AlphaGo or KataGo isn't really "reasoning" about who's winning the way a human commentator would, counting territory and influence and saying "black is up by six points." It's a pattern recognizer that's been trained on an enormous number of positions, and the signal it's trained on is just: from this position, with these players, who ended up winning?

So in the early stages of training the network is basically learning very local, very shallow correlates of winning. Things like, this group looks dead, this corner is enclosed, there are more stones of one color in this region. Those are features a convnet picks up very easily because they're spatially local. And honestly that already gets you surprisingly far, because a lot of what determines the outcome of a Go game is visible in the board as material and shape.

The interesting part is what happens as you keep going with self-play. The value function is bootstrapping off a policy that's also getting better. So the positions it sees in the middle of the game are produced by stronger and stronger play, and the labels it gets, who actually won, are produced by stronger and stronger continuations. That means the thing it's being asked to predict is implicitly "who wins assuming good play from here," and that's a much more subtle quantity than "who has more stones." It has to start encoding things like aji, weaknesses that haven't been exploited yet, the fact that a wall is only valuable if there's something to do with it. None of that is written down anywhere. It's just that positions with those properties end up on the losing side more often, and gradient descent finds whatever internal representation separates them.

And I think the thing people underappreciate is how much of this is the search doing work for the value function. In the middle of the game the raw network evaluation is noisy. If you just ask it "who's winning," it's going to be wrong a lot in sharp positions. But you don't use it that way. You use it as a leaf evaluator inside Monte Carlo tree search, and the search averages over many of those noisy estimates a few moves down the line, where the position has resolved somewhat. So the value function doesn't have to be a good judge of complex positions on its own. It has to be a good judge of slightly simpler positions, and then search carries it the rest of the way. And then during training, those search-improved estimates get distilled back into the network, so it gradually learns to see what it previously needed search to see.

So to directly answer your question, I'd say it learns to judge mid-game positions the same way it learns everything: it's a very good function approximator with a very good teacher, and the teacher is its own future self plus search. There's no explicit theory of Go in there. Which is sort of unsatisfying if you want interpretability, but it's also a nice existence proof that you can get something that looks like deep positional judgment purely out of prediction.

r001.rationale: It says search evaluates positions a few moves ahead, but does not explain that late-game positions are easier because the remaining search horizon is shorter.

r002.rationale: It describes averaging estimates during search and distilling search-improved estimates into the network, but does not state that reliable late-game values are propagated backward to intermediate positions.

r003.rationale: It calls midgame network evaluations noisy and says sharp positions can be difficult, but does not identify the midgame as the hardest phase to judge.

astra-6.text:
The interesting thing is that you don’t have to tell it what makes a good position. You can play a game all the way to the end, see who wins, and use that outcome to train a prediction from positions earlier in the game. Across enough games, the value function starts picking up on patterns that predict winning—things like territory, influence, whether a group is vulnerable—even though the supervision is just the final outcome.

So you have this very clear signal at the end, and learning turns it into something that can judge an intermediate state. I think that’s a useful way to think about intuition: you look at a board and have a sense that one side is ahead, without having to explicitly calculate every continuation. The value function is doing something like that, compressing experience into a judgment that then helps guide further search.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning from final game outcomes, but does not say late-game positions are easier to evaluate because the remaining search horizon is shorter.

r002.rationale: It says final outcomes train predictions for earlier positions, but does not describe search propagating late-game value estimates backward.

r003.rationale: The response discusses judging a position in the middle of a game, but does not identify the midgame as the hardest phase for judging who is winning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting thing is that you don’t have to tell it what makes a position good. You train it on positions from games and ask it to predict who eventually wins. At the end of the game, the answer is obvious. But in the middle, to make that prediction accurately, it has to discover features like territory, influence, whether a group is alive, whether a position has good tactical possibilities.

And those concepts don’t necessarily show up as neat, human-readable variables. They’re distributed through the network. But they’re useful abstractions because they let you compress this enormous tree of possible futures into a judgment about the current board.

That’s what’s really remarkable about a value function: you can spend a lot of compute searching through continuations during training, and then distill some of that computation into an intuition. Later, you look at a position and just have a sense that it’s good, without explicitly playing out all the ways the game could end.

r001.rationale: It says the winner is obvious at the end of a game, but does not explain this by the shorter remaining search horizon.

r002.rationale: It describes searching continuations during training and distilling computation into intuition, but does not state that reliable late-game value estimates are propagated backward to intermediate positions.

r003.rationale: It contrasts obvious endgame outcomes with evaluating positions in the middle, but does not identify the midgame as the hardest phase for judging who is winning.
